_comment: How each place of the catalogue's words-17.jsonl was settled before it went in config/figures-seen/: two readers read every place against its BSB verse, one asking whether the figure is plainly there and one whether the marked words, form and tags are right; a place both passed is kept as handed over, and any place either questioned was read a third time and kept, changed or dropped. A new form stands only where a reader proposed it. Places not read are held, not listed. Stray punctuation before marked words is trimmed, and Strong's tags that light the article (G3588) or the object marker (H0853), or number eight, the search's limit, are taken off as a stretch of words.

Then every kept place marked as said twice was read again by two readers, a third settling any difference: each kept, moved to the form its lines plainly show (a judge's form only where a reader proposed it), or dropped ("label").

Then every kept place marked as lines that begin alike was read again by two readers, a third settling any difference: each kept, cut to the entries that begin with the same words (two or more, in its own verses), or dropped where only one of its lines begins with them or the shared beginning is only a joining word ("beginnings").

Then kept figures of speech were read again by two readers, a third settling any difference ("words re-read" counts them: those a sample showed at risk, such as wide spans, or those found only in the Hebrew or Greek that carry no tags): each kept as it was, cut to the words that carry the figure, or dropped ("words").

Last, a sample of 25 kept places was read by two more readers, a third settling any split; the file goes in only when 24 or more pass, and any place that fails is dropped. "samples" lists each sample and its result.
A place whose verse already has the same form from an earlier file is left out here, since the earlier file's place stands ("same form already on this verse").

places.words_why: "I swore with an uplifted hand" gives God a raised hand. The figure is the hand, so the verb "I swore" is cut.
"Because I swore with an uplifted hand" gives God a raised hand. Only the hand carries the figure.

places.why: "in His sight" is the ordinary English way of saying "before Him". The Aramaic is qodamohi, "before him", with no eyes in it, so no human part or feeling is plainly given to God.

The marked span runs over five poetry lines and stops mid-line at "His throne", so these are not the words of a figure. What Daniel saw in a vision is reported as he saw it. Whether "the hair of His head" is a figure is not plain.
The BSB says "we have not sought the favor of the LORD", so no human part shows in the English. The face is only in the Hebrew, and one tag points at the name Yahweh, which is not the figure.

"He will remember their guilt" reads plainly as God calling sin to account, set beside "He will punish their sins". It names no human part or feeling, and nothing in the words marks it as said in human terms.

places.words_why: "He will roar like a lion" is a plain likeness with "like". The likeness is "roar like a lion", so "He will" is cut.

places.why: "The LORD will roar from Zion" pictures a lion's roar (compare Amos 3:8), not a human part or feeling. The human words "raise His voice" are not marked, and as marked the figure is not plain.
"The LORD roars from Zion" pictures a lion's roar (Amos 3:8), not a human part or feeling. "raises His voice" is not marked. As marked, the figure is not plain.
"reveals His thoughts to man" gives God no human part or feeling, and the Hebrew mah-secho ("what his thought is") could even mean man's thought. The marked words do not carry the figure.
"for I will pass through your midst" reads plainly as the LORD coming in judgment (compare Exodus 12:12). It names no human part or feeling, so the figure is not plain.
"I hate, I despise" plainly says human passions of God. "your feasts" is only what He hates, so the marked words are cut to the two verbs.

"So the LORD relented from this plan" plainly tells what God did after Amos pleaded. "Relented" is a decision, not a body part or a feeling. Calling it a figure means weighing it against verses that say God does not change His mind, and that is commentary work, so it is dropped.

This is the same wording as 7:3: "So the LORD relented from this plan." The BSB gives a plain account of God holding back judgment. A reader would not see this as human terms said of God unless a commentary told them, so it is dropped.
"Behold, the Lord was standing by a wall... with a plumb line in His hand" reports what Amos was shown in a vision. It describes the sight, not a figure of speech a reader would see in the words.

"the eyes of the Lord GOD" plainly gives God eyes, and the tags are on "eyes of" (H5869A) and "Lord" (H0136). The marked words stopped halfway through the title "Lord GOD", so they now take in the whole title.

The BSB's "banished from Your sight" reads as "from Your presence". The Hebrew "from before Your eyes" would carry the figure, but this place has no tags on that word, so the figure is not shown at these words.

"God may turn and relent" is the king of Nineveh hoping God will hold back. In the BSB, "turn" and "relent" mean a change of course, not a human body part or feeling. Reading the words as a figure needs a doctrinal judgment, so when in doubt it is dropped.

"One who relents from sending disaster" is Jonah naming God's mercy alongside "gracious and compassionate." The verse states it as true of God. Whether "relents" is a human term used of Him is a doctrinal reading that the word does not plainly show, so it is dropped.

A staff is a shepherd's tool, not a human part or feeling. The plain figure is a metaphor: God is asked to shepherd His people, who are called "the flock of Your inheritance". The place moves to metaphor, marked on those two lines.
places.words_why: "Shepherd with Your staff Your people, the flock of Your inheritance" plainly calls God's people a flock and His care shepherding. "Your people" is the plain word, not the figure, so the first mark is cut to "Shepherd with Your staff".

places.why: The verse plainly gives God indignation, burning anger and wrath. The marked span took in both questions and stopped partway through a line, so only the three carriers are marked now.
"The cup in the LORD’s right hand" plainly gives God a right hand. The stray "in" is dropped. The tags on yamin and Yahweh mark that same phrase.

"Your bow" names a weapon, not a human part or feeling. The warrior picture (perhaps lightning as arrows) could just as well be metaphor, so the form is in doubt. This matches the drops of "My sword" and "My bow" elsewhere.

"on the Day of the LORD's wrath" and "by the fire of His jealousy" say God's wrath and jealousy outright. Nothing in the verse shows them to be a human feeling said only in a figure. That is a reading some hold and others reject, so with no writer behind it, it should not go live.

"before the burning anger of the LORD comes upon you, before the Day of the LORD's anger" names God's anger as real and coming in judgment. The BSB gives no sign that the anger is a figure, and there are no tags to show a body word behind it.

"Perhaps you will be sheltered on the day of the LORD's anger" speaks of God's anger plainly. The verse does not mark it as a manner of speaking, and whether His anger is a figure at all is something readers differ on.
"I have heard the reproach of Moab" is read plainly as the LORD knowing of the taunts. No ear or human limit is in view, and the span also takes in the object.
"slain by My sword" names a weapon, which is not a human part, feeling or action. It most likely stands for the war God brings through others, so the figure is not plainly this one.

In "to pour out upon them My indignation, all My burning anger" God speaks of His own indignation. Nothing in the words shows it to be a human feeling said only in a figure, so a reader would need a commentary to see this figure.
"The LORD was very angry with your fathers" is a plain statement of God's anger. Nothing in the verse shows it is a manner of speaking rather than a true account of Him, so the figure is not plain.
"with which You have been angry these seventy years" says God's anger outright. The words do not mark it as figurative, and reading it as a figure is a matter of interpretation.

The speaker of "I will surely wave My hand over them" goes on: "Then you will know that the LORD of Hosts has sent Me." He is one sent by the LORD, and readers differ on who he is, so it is not plain that "My hand" is a human part said of God.
"His throne" belongs to "a man whose name is the Branch" (6:12). That is a king's throne, not a human part or feeling said of God.

The BSB has "to plead before the LORD" and shows no face. The Hebrew "entreat the face of Yahweh" is a stock idiom for asking favor, and the translators rendered it as such, so the figure is not plain enough to stand with no name behind it.

"I am jealous for Zion with great zeal; I am jealous for her with great fervor" is God stating His own jealousy. The verse does not show it to be a figure, and calling it a human feeling only said of Him is a reading some would reject.
The LORD of Hosts asks "should it also be impossible in My eyes?", setting His eyes against "the eyes of the remnant". The BSB shows eyes said of God, and the span is exact.

"when your fathers provoked Me to anger, and I did not relent" says God was angered. Nothing in the words marks this as a figure, so whether His anger is only said in human terms is left to interpretation.

"My bow" alone is not a human part or feeling of God. The plain figure, "I will bend Judah as My bow", is a likeness, and this verse already has its own simile place.
"My anger burns against the shepherds" is God speaking of His anger. The verse does not show the anger itself to be a figure, and "burns" would be another figure, not this one.
"I will refine them" is not a human part or feeling of God. The plain figure, "like silver" and "like gold", is a likeness, and this verse already has its own simile place.
"His feet will stand on the Mount of Olives" is read by many Bible-believing readers as a literal, bodily coming (compare Acts 1:11-12). Whether it is a figure at all is in real doubt.

"ask now for God’s favor" renders the stock idiom "entreat the face of God" and shows no face in the BSB. The second span, "will He show you favor", renders the people's faces, not God's, and is untagged. Doubtful, so it is dropped.

"every word that comes from the mouth of God" plainly gives God a mouth, in the BSB as well as the Greek. The span was the whole verse and is cut to the carrier. The tags on stomatos and theou are right.
"remembering to be merciful" uses remembering in the Bible's ordinary sense of God keeping His promise. It is not plainly a figure, and the span also takes in "to be merciful".

"For the Lord’s hand was with him" plainly gives God a hand, in the BSB as well as the Greek. The span was the whole verse, including the people's question, and is cut to the carrier. The tags on cheir and kuriou are right.
"to remember His holy covenant" reads plainly as God keeping His covenant, not as a figure. The span also takes in the object.

"God rested from all His works" can be read plainly as God ceasing from His finished work, and a careful reader would not see a human action said of God here without a commentary telling him.

In the BSB "a still, small voice" is just a quiet voice, and no words clash. Any clash is only in the Hebrew, and the place has no tags.
"miserable comforters are you all" is Job's bitter charge that his friends comfort badly. Nothing in it seems foolish yet proves wise, and no other form is plain enough.
"My friends are my scoffers" is a plain complaint. No words clash and nothing seems foolish yet proves wise.
"Even in laughter the heart may ache" is a plain observation that laughter can hide pain. It does not seem foolish, so it is not plainly a paradox.
"by His stripes we are healed" states the substitution plainly, as the parallel lines "pierced for our transgressions" show. Calling it a seeming contradiction is a reading only some would bring.
"buried like a donkey" is a likeness with "like", not a paradox. The simile is already marked as jeremiah-22-19-simile-seen ("like a donkey"), so moving this place to simile would make a duplicate.
"their shouts are not for joy" plainly says the joyful harvest shouts have stopped. Nothing in the BSB seems foolish yet proves wise, and the place has no tags.
Calling people blessed when they are insulted and persecuted is plainly a paradox. The old mark stopped before the words that make the clash.
places.words_why: "Blessed are you when people insult you" plainly calls the insulted blessed. The marked words stop partway through the list at "persecute you", so the shortest whole phrase is kept.

places.why: Losing one's life to save it is plainly a paradox. "loses his life" alone does not carry it, so the mark is the whole clause through "will save it".
Calling the hated blessed is plainly a paradox. The old mark stopped before "hate you", which makes the clash.
Losing one's life to save it is plainly a paradox. The mark must run through "will save it".
Losing one's life to preserve it is plainly a paradox. The mark must run through "will preserve it".
Hating one's life in order to keep it is plainly a paradox. "hates his life" alone does not show it, so the mark is the whole clause.
Invisible qualities that have been clearly seen is a plain clash. The mark needs both sides of it.
"Against all hope, Abraham in hope believed" plainly sets hope against hope. "Against all hope" alone does not show the clash.
places.words_why: "Against all hope, Abraham in hope believed" plainly sets hope against hope. The clash is in "Against all hope" and "in hope", so the name and the verb between and after them are left out.

places.why: People set free who have become slaves is a plain clash. The mark needs the freedom as well as the slavery.
Being set free and becoming slaves to God is a plain clash. The mark needs both sides.
The slave is the Lord's freedman and the free man is Christ's slave, a plain reversal. The mark needs each side of both halves.
Free yet a slave to everyone is said of one man at once, a plain clash. It needs both halves, so the marked words become the whole clause.
places.words_why: "Though I am free of obligation to anyone, I make myself a slave to everyone" plainly sets freedom against slavery. The clash is carried by the two phrases.

places.why: "hard pressed on all sides, but not crushed" sets a limit on a hardship. Nothing in it contradicts itself, and "but not crushed" alone carries no figure.
"persecuted, but not forsaken" says how far the trouble went. It is a contrast of degree, not a statement that seems to contradict itself.
Seen against unseen, and temporary against eternal, are plain opposites set together. Calling it a paradox is open to doubt, so it goes under antithesis, with both pairs marked.

"unknown, yet well-known" and "dying, and yet we live on" plainly say clashing things of the same people. The marked "unknown, yet" broke off before the other half. "punished, yet not killed" is only a limit, so it is left out.
Each pair plainly sets clashing things side by side. The marked "sorrowful, yet" cut off the second half, so the three whole pairs are marked.
The clash is that others are made rich through His poverty. "for your sakes He became poor" on its own is only a change of state.
Power made perfect in weakness is a plain clash. The marked words left out "power", which is half of it.
Knowing a love that is beyond knowing is a plain paradox. The marked words left out "to know", which is half of the clash.

"Their glory is in their shame" puts two clashing words together, but it condemns people who boast in what should shame them. Nothing in it seems foolish and then proves wise, which is what this form means. A reader would sooner see irony or opposites here, so with doubt about the label, it does not go live.
"I rejoice in my sufferings for you" plainly states an attitude, and the verse gives its reason. Nothing in the words contradicts itself.
"in spite of your great suffering" states the contrast outright, a plain concession and not a figure. The marked words also end on a dangling "in spite of".
Dead while still alive is a plain contradiction in words. The marked "dead even while" stopped before the other half.
"joyfully accepted the confiscation" reports what they did, and the reason follows at once. The words do not contradict each other.
Seeing the invisible is a plain paradox. Without "saw", the marked words only describe God.
In this list of deeds, "gained strength from weakness" reads as a change from weak to strong, not as a contradiction.
"Consider it pure joy ... when you encounter trials" is a plain command, and verse 3 gives the reason. It is not a figure of clashing words, and the marked words also take in "my brothers".
Christ is plainly called "the living stone", which a reader sees first as a metaphor. Calling it an oxymoron is open to doubt, so it goes under metaphor. The marked words carry the figure.
"like living stones" is a likeness with "like", a plain simile, so it goes under simile with "like" included in the marked words.
The verse is a plain rule against misusing freedom, so freedom and service are not set up as a clash. The marked "live as servants of God" is also only half.
"rejoice that you share in the sufferings of Christ" is a plain command with its reason in the same verse. The words do not clash as a figure.

The clash is only between verses: 2:7 says "not ... a new commandment, but an old one" and 2:8 says "I am also writing to you a new commandment". The words marked in 2:8 do not carry it alone, so a reader would see only "a new commandment" lit.
The whole verse is marked, and the BSB "poured undiluted" shows no clash. The "mixed unmixed" reading is only in the Greek, with no Strong's tags on those words, and the note leans on a commentator.

Each name taking up the one before is simply how a genealogy is written. No line goes a step higher in force or sense.
This is the ordinary father-to-son chain of a genealogy, with no step up in emphasis, so it is not climbing lines.
This is a list of generations in the genealogy's ordinary chain. The lines do not rise in force from one to the next.

"Salmon was the father of Boaz by Rahab, Boaz the father of Obed by Ruth, Obed the father of Jesse" is how a genealogy normally links its names. Each line goes down one generation, not a step higher in force or sense, so these are not climbing lines.

"Solomon the father of Rehoboam, Rehoboam the father of Abijah, and Abijah the father of Asa" is the genealogy's fixed chain. The names are taken up only to record descent, with no rise in emphasis, so this is not plainly climbing.
"Asa was the father of Jehoshaphat, Jehoshaphat the father of Joram, and Joram the father of Uzziah" is the ordinary father-to-son chain of a genealogy. No line goes higher than the one before it.

"Uzziah was the father of Jotham, Jotham the father of Ahaz, and Ahaz the father of Hezekiah" is the genealogy's stock form. The repeated names carry the line of descent, not any rise in emphasis or sense, so this is not climbing.

"Hezekiah was the father of Manasseh, Manasseh the father of Amon, Amon the father of Josiah" is the list of generations in its usual chain. Nothing goes a step higher, so this is not plainly climbing.

The second line, "at the time of the exile to Babylon", repeats no word of "and Josiah the father of Jeconiah and his brothers". It only gives the time, so even the chain shape is missing here, and the genealogy's chain is not climbing anyway.

"Zerubbabel the father of Abiud, Abiud the father of Eliakim, and Eliakim the father of Azor" is the genealogy's fixed formula. There is no step up in emphasis or sense, so this is not climbing lines.
"Azor was the father of Zadok, Zadok the father of Achim, and Achim the father of Eliud" is how the list of generations runs all through the chapter. It is a stock form, not lines that rise in force.

"Eliud was the father of Eleazar, Eleazar the father of Matthan, Matthan the father of Jacob" is the ordinary chain of a genealogy. Names are taken up only to record descent, with no rise in emphasis, so this is not plainly climbing.

"of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ" takes up none of the words of "and Jacob the father of Joseph, the husband of Mary" and goes no step higher. The X-father-of-Y chain is just how a genealogy speaks, so it is not a figure.
